candidates.text: That's the right separation: velocity error at the boundary  -  order 1e-3 to 1e-2 km/s depending on body and kernel  -  is a magnitude problem in the translational state, while the IAU frame DCM is an orientation problem, and conflating the two is how people misdiagnose a rotation bug as a propagation bug. Keep the DCM out of the Monte Carlo on position/velocity entirely; it's deterministic per epoch from the PCK, so any scatter you see in attitude-dependent quantities must come from your own rotation chain, not from SPICE's ephemeris uncertainty. Carrying it separately also means you can validate it independently  -  diff the DCM against a second PCK vintage the same way you'd diff spkpos outputs, instead of burying a frame error inside what looks like a velocity residual.

That DCM split assumes the rotation and the translation fail independently, but frame bias and ephemeris bias both trace back to the same JPL solution  -  so the velocity residual you're chasing at the boundary might just be the position error's time-derivative wearing an attitude costume. Try the opposite isolation: hold the IAU DCM fixed and swap only the SPK kernel, and see if the "velocity glitch" survives  -  if it vanishes, you were never looking at a rotation problem at all. A boundary artifact that disappears when you change the translation input was never a frame issue to begin with.

If your M7 workbench or Simulink model is doing anything with money, exact thresholds, or accumulated small steps, that's precisely where float error compounds silently across iterations. The fix isn't vocabulary, it's choosing fixed-point or decimal types at the one or two places where exactness actually matters.

candidates.text: Selfish gene reconstruction is Dawkins' replicator logic run backward: you infer the ancestral allele state that maximizes its own transmission, not the one that best explains organismal form, and that's a cleaner instance of the same labeling problem you flagged with M7.1  -  the gene is the unit of selection, the organism is just the container. That's the same category split as header-versus-float: ancestral-state reconstruction done at the phenotype level answers "what did this creature look like," while done at the gene level it answers "what sequence propagated itself," and conflating the two gives you a tree that's internally consistent but answering the wrong question. If you want this grounded rather than circling, the concrete move is to specify which unit  -  allele frequency or organismal trait  -  the reconstruction algorithm is actually optimizing over, because that choice is what turns an ambiguous label into a falsifiable model, the same resolution "installing the app" gave you a moment ago.

Selfish gene logic says genes build phylogenetic trees to track their own replication, but ancestral reconstruction only works backward because mutation is close to clock-like  -  swap that assumption and the whole method inverts. Try this displacement: a "selfish" unit doesn't need a coherent ancestor at all, it just needs differential persistence, so the tree you reconstruct might be an artifact of your inference method imposing bifurcation on what was actually reticulate horizontal transfer. The real question isn't whose gene won, it's whether "ancestor" is doing the same category-work here that "float versus header" did a minute ago  -  a label mistaken for a mechanism.

candidates.text: Non-recursive is the operative term: a self-improvement loop that doesn't feed its own output back as training signal can still compound across passes without the runaway-divergence risk, which is exactly the right constraint for pipelines doing physical simulation. Oklo viewer, Matt Lab, and basil skin optics each sit on lizard or OpenFOAM solvers where the ground truth is a measured field, not a generated one  -  so each pass gets corrected against reality instead of against its own prior guess. That's the coherent design: improvement bounded by an external referent at every iteration, not a chain of self-referential polish.

That's actually closer to how biological surface patterns evolve anyway  -  lizard scales and basil cuticle ridges aren't optimizing an optimizer, they're each separately selected against a fixed fitness landscape, generation by generation, with no meta-level recursion at all. The overlooked move is treating "non-recursive" as the safety property you want across a heterogeneous pipeline stack, not a limitation you're stuck with until something gets smarter.

An orderbook is a cycle by nature  -  bids and asks continuously revise each other, every match feeds back into the next quote  -  while a balance engine wants to be the acyclic ledger underneath it, a strict append-only tree of settled state with zero Tarjan bridges to argue about after the fact.
